questions.stem: Loss of function mutation of which gene is responsible for the majority of cases of Hirschsprung's disease:
questions.solutionHtml:
RET
  • The loss of function mutation of the RET gene is responsible for the majority of cases of Hirschsprung's disease.
  • RET is a proto-oncogene that plays a crucial role in the development of the enteric nervous system, which controls the motility of the gastrointestinal tract.
  • Mutations in RET can lead to abnormal migration or differentiation of the ENS precursor cells during fetal development, resulting in the absence or reduction of ganglion cells in the distal colon and rectum.
  • This leads to a functional obstruction of the affected bowel segment, causing symptoms such as constipation, abdominal distension, and vomiting.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 608,609

questions.stem: Which statement regarding Hirschsprung's disease is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Occurs due to the absence of neural crest cell migration

options.label: B
options.text: Absence of ganglion cells in the affected segment

options.label: D
options.text: Intraoperative frozen section done to confirm the diagnosis

questions.solutionHtml:
Rectum is always spared
  • Hirschsprung disease results when the normal migration of neural crest cells from the cecum to the rectum is arrested prematurely or when the ganglion cells undergo premature death.
  • The rectum can be involved in Hirschsprung's disease, depending on the extent of aganglionosis.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 608-609

questions.stem: Which of the following is a histological feature commonly seen in Barrett's esophagus?

options.label: A
options.text: Squamous epithelium with basal cell hyperplasia

questions.solutionHtml:
Columnar epithelium with goblet cells
  • Barrett's esophagus is a complication of chronic GERD that is characterized by intestinal metaplasia within the esophageal squamous mucosa.
  • There is the replacement of the normal squamous epithelium of the esophagus with a columnar epithelium containing goblet cells.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 595

questions.stem: All of the following are true regarding histological features of Barrett's esophagus except:

options.label: B
options.text: Sub-Classified based on length of involvement

options.label: D
options.text: Dysplastic cells invade the lamina propria

questions.answerText: Dysplastic cells invade the lamina propria
questions.solutionHtml:
Dysplastic cells invade the lamina propria

Dysplasia is a premalignant change that can be seen in the epithelium of Barrett's esophagus, but dysplastic cells do not invade the lamina propria.



Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 595

questions.stem: Which special stain is performed to confirm the diagnosis of Barrett's esophagus:
questions.solutionHtml:
AB-PAS

ABPAS (Alcian blue & PAS) is the most commonly used stain to identify the type of mucus secretion and confirmation of the histological diagnosis of Barrett's esophagus.



Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 595

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old patient had repeated episodes of reflux and burning pain for a prolonged duration. An esophageal biopsy was performed and shown below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Barrett esophagus

The given clinical history with the histopathological image is suggestive of intestinal metaplasia i.e. replacement of the squamous esophageal epithelium with goblet cells that points to the diagnosis of Barrett's esophagus.



Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 595

questions.stem: Which is the most common benign tumour of esophagus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Leiomyoma

Benign tumours of the esophagus are generally mesenchymal, and arise within the esophageal wall, with leiomyomas being the most common.



Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 596,597

questions.stem: All of the following statements are true regarding adenocarcinoma of esophagus except:

options.label: B
options.text: It occurs in the upper esophagus

options.label: C
options.text: Mutation of TP53 and p16/INK4a is seen

options.label: D
options.text: Tumor cell most commonly produces mucin and forms glands

questions.answerText: It occurs in the upper esophagus
questions.solutionHtml:
It occurs in the upper esophagus
  • Adenocarcinoma usually occurs in the lower esophagus or gastroesophageal junction, not in the upper esophagus.
  • It is a type of cancer that typically arises from Barrett's esophagus, a condition in which the normal squamous epithelium of the lower esophagus is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium.
  • The tumour cells of adenocarcinoma often produce mucin and form glandular structures.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 596

questions.stem: Which of the following genetic mutations is commonly found in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma?
questions.solutionHtml:
TP53
  • Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma is commonly associated with TP53 mutations.
  • TP53 encodes the tumour suppressor protein p53, which plays a crucial role in cell cycle regulation, DNA repair, and apoptosis.
  • Mutations in TP53 can lead to loss of p53 function, resulting in uncontrolled cell growth and tumorigenesis.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 596,597

questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old has a prolonged history of alcohol and tobacco chewing and presented with symptoms of dysphagia. A mass lesion was seen on the barium meal in the esophagus. Esophageal biopsy was taken and shown below, what is your diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Squamous cell carcinoma

The given clinical scenario and a histopathological image showing keratin pearls are suggestive of Squamous cell carcinoma.



Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 596,597

questions.stem: In the case of gastric adenocarcinoma metastasis to the axilla is known as:
questions.solutionHtml:
Irish node

An Irish node is an enlarged axillary lymph node caused by metastasis, often associated with gastric adenocarcinoma.



Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 596,597

questions.stem: Which of the following proteins is associated with the development of diffuse gastric carcinoma?
questions.solutionHtml:
E cadherin
  • E-cadherin is a calcium-dependent cell adhesion protein that plays an important role in maintaining the integrity of epithelial cell layers
  • Loss of its expression is thought to promote the progression of cancer by disrupting the adhesion between cells.
  • In diffuse gastric carcinoma, there is often a germline or somatic mutation in the CDH1 gene, which encodes for E-cadherin, leading to its loss of expression.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 605,606

questions.stem: All of the following statements are true regarding diffuse gastric carcinoma except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Gland formation seen
  • Diffuse gastric cancer is generally composed of discohesive cells, likely as a result of  E-cadherin loss.  
  • These cells do not form glands but instead have large mucin vacuoles that expand the cytoplasm and push the nucleus to the periphery, creating a signet-ring cell morphology.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 605,606

questions.stemHtml: Based on the classical histological picture identify the type of tumour:
questions.solutionHtml:
Signet ring cell carcinoma
  • The histopathological image showing cells with large mucin vacuoles that are expanding the cytoplasm and pushing the nucleus to the periphery suggests the diagnosis of signet ring cell carcinoma.



Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 605,606

questions.stem: All of the following statements are true regarding gastric lymphoma except:

options.label: A
options.text: MALToma is the most common type of lymphoma

options.label: C
options.text: There is an increase in the activity of NF-kB

questions.solutionHtml:
It is T-cell lymphoma

Gastric lymphoma is a type of lymphoma that originates in the stomach. These are usually extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma and not T-cell lymphoma.



Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 605,606

questions.stem: Carney Stratakis syndrome is associated with a mutation in which gene:
questions.solutionHtml:
SDH
  • Carney-Stratakis syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic condition that predisposes individuals to develop gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) and paragangliomas.
  • It is caused by germline mutations in the succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) genes, which are involved in the mitochondrial electron transport chain.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 605,606

questions.stem: What is the origin of Gastrointestinal stromatolites tumour?
questions.solutionHtml:
GI pacemaker cells
  • Gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) are believed to arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC) or their precursors.
  • The ICC are specialized cells that are essential for the regulation of gastrointestinal motility and electrical rhythmicity.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 605,606

questions.stem: The IHC marker diagnostic of GIST is:
questions.solutionHtml:
CD 117
  • The most useful diagnostic marker is KIT (CD 117) which is detectable in Cajal cells and 95% of gastric GISTs by immunohistochemical stains.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 605,606
